theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you rework a board from a customer's alarm panel, what should you find out first?
options: Its solder type and the maker's rework rules
The price that the customer first paid for the whole panel
How many boards the maker sold last year
Which colour the board's solder mask is

questions.stem: A faulty board must be taken out of a 220 V control panel for repair. What comes first?
options: Unplug the board's ribbon cable while it runs
Isolate, lock off and prove the panel dead
Switch the panel off at its front switch only
Spray the board with cleaner to cool it down

questions.stem: Why must the large capacitors on a power supply board be checked for stored charge before you solder on it?
options: They lose their value if they are charged
Charged capacitors cannot be de-soldered from a board at all
They can hold a dangerous charge after power is off
They make the solder flow much too quickly

questions.stem: Where should the intake of a fume extractor be placed when soldering?
options: On the floor under the bench, out of the way
Behind your head so it pulls air past your face
On the far side of the room near the window
Close to the joint, drawing fumes away from you

questions.stem: Why should you never flick extra solder off the iron tip?
options: Molten solder can hit eyes or skin
The tip will lose its temperature
The solder can no longer be used
The flux will turn into a gas

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the resistor (often about 1 MΩ) built into a wrist strap lead?
options: It makes the strap more comfortable to wear
It limits current through you if you touch a live part
It stops the strap from building up any static
It lets the strap work well without any earth connection at all

questions.stem: How should a wrist strap be checked before a session of work on sensitive parts?
options: By pulling the lead to see if it is strong
By rubbing it on a carpet to see if it sparks
With a strap tester, and the result recorded
By looking at it to see that it is clean

questions.stem: Which bench item helps carry static away safely in a static-safe work area?
options: A thick rubber mat that is not earthed
A sheet of shiny metal foil left loose
A plastic tray for the parts and tools
A dissipative mat connected to earth

questions.stem: Which item should NOT be brought onto a static-safe bench?
options: Ordinary plastic bags and foam cups
Anti-static bags holding new parts
An earthed soldering station
A dissipative bench mat

questions.stem: Why is 63/37 tin-lead solder often preferred to 60/40 for hand soldering?
options: It contains no lead at all
It sets at once, with no pasty stage
It melts at a much higher temperature
It needs no flux to make a good joint

questions.stem: About what temperature does a common lead-free tin-silver-copper solder melt?
options: About 183 °C
About 150 °C
About 217–220 °C
About 300 °C

questions.stem: How does a good lead-free joint usually look, compared with a good tin-lead joint?
options: Bright, like a mirror
Black and burnt
Raised up in a ball
A little duller and less shiny

questions.stem: Why should lead-free and tin-lead solder not be mixed on the same joint unless the maker allows it?
options: The mix can form a weaker joint that may crack
The two solders will change the joint's colour
The iron will need to be twice as hot as normal
The joint will not conduct electricity at all

questions.stem: Why should the tip temperature not be set much higher than the job needs?
options: The solder will set before it reaches the pad
It burns the flux and can lift pads or harm parts
The joint will be far too shiny to inspect properly afterwards
The iron will switch itself off after a minute

questions.stem: A large earth pad on a power board will not take solder with a fine conical tip. What is the best fix?
options: Hold the fine tip on the pad for a full minute
Turn the station to its highest setting
Use a larger chisel tip or a more powerful iron
Scrape the pad with a sharp knife to make the copper thinner

questions.stem: Why may a thick multilayer board need preheating before rework?
options: So the green solder mask turns a darker colour before work
So static is removed from the board
So the parts can be seen more clearly
Its copper layers draw heat away from the joint

questions.stem: How can you check that a soldering station's real tip temperature matches its display?
options: With a tip thermometer, as the maker says
By touching the tip quickly with a wet finger
By timing how fast the solder wire melts
By watching the colour of the tip change

questions.stem: The tip of a plated soldering iron has gone black and will not take solder. What should you do?
options: File it back to bare copper and use it
Clean it with tip tinner or brass wool, then re-tin it
Dip it in cold water to crack the black layer off the tip quickly
Turn the station up higher until solder sticks

questions.stem: Why should the iron be turned down or set to sleep when it will not be used for a while?
options: So the stand does not get dusty
So the cable does not tangle up
It makes the tip last much longer
So the flux in the solder dries out

questions.stem: A board was soldered with water-soluble flux. What must be done afterwards?
options: Leave the residue on, as it helps to protect the board from damp
Paint over the residue with clear varnish
Bake the board in an oven to harden it
Clean the residue off, as it can corrode the board

questions.stem: What does 'no-clean' flux mean?
options: Its residue may be left on, if the job allows
It does not clean the metal at all
It must never be used on any kind of circuit board
It cleans the iron tip as you solder

questions.stem: When is it useful to add liquid or gel flux before reworking a joint?
options: Only when using brand-new solder wire
When reflowing old joints or clearing bridges
Only on joints that already look perfect
Never, as cored solder holds all the flux needed

questions.stem: On a plated through-hole joint, what shows that the solder has flowed properly?
options: A large ball of solder sits on top of the lead
The solder is only on the side you soldered
It fills the hole and wets the pads on both sides
The lead has turned black where it enters the hole

questions.stem: Which fault is caused by using too much solder on a joint?
options: The lead is left loose in the hole
The copper pad lifts away from the board around the lead
The flux turns brown and sticky
Solder hides the lead's outline and may bridge

questions.stem: A through-hole joint has too little solder and the hole is only half filled. What should be done?
options: Add flux and solder, and reheat to fill it
Leave it, as half a hole is strong enough
Push the lead further in while it is cold
Glue the lead in place with epoxy

questions.stem: What usually causes a small blowhole (pinhole) in a through-hole joint?
options: A tip that is too big for the joint
Gas or moisture escaping from the hole
Solder wire that is too thin
Using a wrist strap while soldering

questions.stem: The board material near a joint has turned brown and blistered after rework. What does this show?
options: The board was static damaged
The flux was the wrong brand
Too much heat, for too long
The joint is very well made

questions.stem: A pad lifts off the board while you are de-soldering. What should a Level 3 technician do?
options: Glue it down and solder over it quickly
Throw the whole board away at once and fit a brand-new one
Hide it under extra solder and carry on
Record it, and repair it by an approved method

questions.stem: Which tool is best for removing a small surface-mount chip resistor?
options: Hot tweezers or a hot-air rework tool
A desoldering pump on each end in turn
A hacksaw blade slid under the part
A large chisel tip pressed on the middle

questions.stem: When hand soldering a two-ended surface-mount part, what is the usual first step?
options: Solder both pads fully, then press the part on
Tin one pad, then place and solder that end first
Glue the part down, then solder both ends at once
Heat the part's middle until both ends flow

questions.stem: A fine-pitch IC has solder bridges between several pins. What is the best fix?
options: Cut between the pins with a sharp knife
Add more solder until all of the bridges join up into one
Add flux and draw the bridges off with braid
Leave them, as the IC will still work

questions.stem: When using a hot-air rework tool, why should nearby parts be shielded?
options: So the air flows faster to the joint
So the board stays clean of flux
So the solder does not change colour
So they are not heated, moved or damaged

questions.stem: A faulty 16-pin through-hole IC will be thrown away. Which removal method protects the board best?
options: Cut its leads, then remove each lead one at a time
Heat all the pins together with a large tip and pull it out hard
Lever it out with a screwdriver while heating
Twist it back and forth until the leads break

questions.stem: Why is the board fixed in a board holder instead of held by hand during rework?
options: So it cannot be seen by the customer
So both hands are free and it does not move
So the board stays warm between joints
So static can build up in the board

questions.stem: Before soldering a wire to a terminal post, what should be done?
options: Push the bare wire against the post and hold it
Coat the post with grease so solder flows
Wrap it partly round the post so it is held
Flatten the wire with pliers first

questions.stem: In power wiring, why should a stranded conductor NOT be tinned with solder before it goes into a screw terminal?
options: The solder stops current flowing through it
Tinned ends are far too thick to fit into any screw terminal
The solder melts when the circuit is used
The solder slowly flattens, so the terminal works loose

questions.stem: Why is a soldered wire joint that will be shaken or vibrated given extra support?
options: Solder stiffens the wire, so it can break at the joint's edge
Solder gets softer each time it is shaken
Vibration makes the solder change into a powder
The joint will get hotter as it vibrates

questions.stem: Which is the best way to insulate a soldered joint between two wires?
options: Several turns of masking tape
Heat-shrink sleeving, shrunk with a heat gun
A blob of hot glue over the joint
Nothing, as solder is an insulator

questions.stem: At work, what are finished solder joints judged against?
options: How the joints on the last board looked
Whatever the person doing the work prefers
The customer's or company's written workmanship standard
The colour of the board's solder mask

questions.stem: After a part is replaced on a 12 V control board, which is the safest first test?
options: Power it from the mains to see if it smokes
Connect it straight into the customer's panel
Tap it with a screwdriver while it is running
Check for shorts with a meter before power-up

questions.stem: When the repaired board is first powered for testing, which supply is best?
options: A current-limited bench supply at its rated voltage
The mains outlet on the bench, through a fuse
A car battery, as it can give plenty of current for the test
Any supply that is higher than the rated voltage

questions.stem: What should a rework record include?
options: Only the date and the board's colour
Board, part changed, fault, tests and who did it
Only the price of the new part fitted
The names of everyone in the workshop

questions.stem: A trainee carries solder to the joint on the iron tip and dabs it on. Why is this poor practice?
options: The solder will be too cold to flow
The tip will become too heavy to hold
The flux burns off before it can clean the joint
The joint will end up with far too much solder on the pad

questions.stem: A trainee holds the iron on a pad for 15 seconds because the solder will not flow. What should you tell him?
options: Keep going, as it will flow if he waits
Press harder on the pad with the tip
Turn the station to its highest setting
Stop, check tip size, clean, flux, then retry

questions.stem: At the end of a soldering session, what should be done with the soldering station?
options: Tip tinned, power off, cooled in its stand, bench clean
Tip wiped dry, left on so it is ready tomorrow
Tip removed and put in a drawer while still hot
Station unplugged and the hot tip laid on the bench

essays.stem: Describe how to set up a static-safe (ESD-safe) soldering workstation, and how you would check that it is working.
essays.modelAnswer: I mark the area as an ESD protected area and keep ordinary plastics, foam cups and paper away from it. The bench has a dissipative mat connected to a common earth point, and the soldering station has an earthed tip. Each worker wears a wrist strap with its built-in resistor of about 1 MΩ, clipped to the earth point, and where the floor is suitable, heel straps or ESD footwear. Sensitive parts stay in their anti-static bags or tubes until they are fitted, and are handled by their edges. Before each session, each wrist strap is tested on a strap tester and the result recorded. The mat's earth lead and the earth point are checked at set times with a suitable meter. Anyone whose strap fails does not handle parts until it is fixed.
markingPoints: Marked area, ordinary plastics kept out
Earthed dissipative mat and earthed iron
Wrist strap with resistor connected to the earth point
Parts kept in protective packaging and handled carefully
Daily strap tests recorded; mat and earth checked; failures acted on

essays.stem: Explain the main differences between tin-lead and lead-free solder for hand soldering and rework, including temperature, joint appearance and inspection.
essays.modelAnswer: Tin-lead solder such as 63/37 melts at about 183 °C and flows easily, so a lower tip temperature can be used. Lead-free solder, usually tin, silver and copper, melts at about 217 to 220 °C, so it needs a higher tip temperature and wets more slowly, which puts more heat into the parts and board. Tips also wear faster with lead-free. A good tin-lead joint is bright and smooth, but a good lead-free joint is often duller and a little grainy, so an inspector must not reject it for that alone; the shape of the fillet and good wetting matter more. The two should not be mixed on one joint unless the maker allows. Tin-lead contains lead, so hand washing and no food at the bench are important, while both need fume extraction.
markingPoints: Melting temperatures of each
Lead-free needs more heat and wets more slowly; tip wear
Joint appearance differs; inspect shape and wetting
Do not mix the two without the maker's approval
Health points: lead hygiene and fume extraction

essays.stem: Describe step by step how to remove a faulty multi-pin through-hole IC from a double-sided board and fit a new one without damaging the board.
essays.modelAnswer: With the board out of the equipment and in a holder at an ESD-safe bench, I note the IC's orientation by its notch or dot. If the IC is faulty and will be scrapped, I cut each lead close to the body and remove the leads one at a time with the iron and tweezers. Otherwise I use a vacuum desoldering tool or pump and braid to clear each hole, adding fresh flux, and check every pin is free before lifting the IC. I never force it out. I clean the holes and pads with braid and flux, inspect for lifted pads or damaged tracks, and repair any damage by an approved method. I fit the new IC the right way round, solder two corner pins, check it is flat, then solder the rest, letting each joint cool. Finally I clean the flux if needed, inspect both sides and test.
markingPoints: ESD-safe set-up and orientation noted
Correct removal method (cut leads if scrapped, or clear each hole)
Never forces the part; checks all pins are free
Cleans and inspects the pads and repairs damage
Fits new IC correctly, solders, inspects both sides and tests

essays.stem: Describe how to hand solder and remove two-ended surface-mount parts, and how to clear solder bridges on a fine-pitch IC.
essays.modelAnswer: To fit a two-ended part, I clean the pads, put a little solder on one pad, then hold the part with tweezers and reheat that pad so the part settles flat in place. I then solder the other end, and finally reflow the first end so both joints are good, with small fillets. To remove a part, I use hot tweezers that heat both ends at once, or a hot-air tool with the right nozzle, shielding nearby parts, and lift the part as soon as both ends melt. For bridges on a fine-pitch IC, I add flux to the pins, then lay solder braid across the bridges and heat it, so the extra solder is drawn off. Sometimes dragging a clean, fluxed tip along the pins clears them. I inspect under magnification and clean the flux if needed.
markingPoints: Tins one pad, places and tacks the part with tweezers
Solders second end and reflows first
Removal with hot tweezers or hot air, shielding nearby parts
Bridges cleared with flux and braid (or drag)
Inspects under magnification and cleans

essays.stem: Explain how you would inspect a reworked board against a workmanship standard: what you look for, the tools you use, and how you record the result.
essays.modelAnswer: I use the customer's or company's written workmanship standard so the judgement is the same each time. I inspect under good light with a magnifier or bench microscope, looking at both sides of the board. For each joint I check good wetting with a smooth fillet, the right amount of solder, solder through plated holes, no bridges, spikes, solder balls or cracks, and no disturbed joints. I check that parts are the right ones, the right way round and seated flat, that leads are trimmed to length, and that the board shows no burning, lifted pads or damaged tracks. I check that flux has been cleaned where required. I record the board's number, what was reworked, any defects found and how they were corrected, the result and my name and date, and I mark the board as passed or rejected.
markingPoints: Uses the written standard
Good light and magnification, both sides
Joint criteria (wetting, amount, fill, bridges, cracks)
Parts, orientation and board damage checked
Records results and marks the board passed or rejected

essays.stem: A power supply board has large copper areas and heavy parts beside small, heat-sensitive ones. Explain how you would plan the soldering so the joints are good and the board is not damaged.
essays.modelAnswer: Large copper areas and heavy leads draw heat away, so a small tip would need too long and give cold joints. I would choose a larger chisel tip or a higher-power iron for the heavy joints, rather than just turning the temperature right up. I might preheat the board gently with a board preheater so the joints reach temperature quickly. For the small, sensitive parts I would use a fine tip and a short contact time, and clip a heat sink on their leads where needed. I would do the heavy joints first and the delicate parts last, so they are not heated again. I would use fresh flux, keep the tip clean and tinned, and check each joint. Afterwards I would inspect for burning or lifted pads and test the board.
markingPoints: Explains why heavy copper needs more heat
Larger tip or more powerful iron, not just higher temperature
Preheating where suitable
Fine tip, short time and heat sinks for sensitive parts; sensible order
Inspects for damage and tests

essays.stem: Explain when soldered connections are suitable in electrical work, and when crimped or screw connections are better.
essays.modelAnswer: Soldering is the normal way to fit electronic parts to circuit boards and to join small signal wires to connectors and terminal posts, where currents are small and the joint is supported. Soldered joints are not suitable where they will be clamped in a screw terminal, because solder slowly flattens under pressure and the terminal works loose and overheats. So stranded conductors going into screw terminals in power wiring get a crimped ferrule, not solder. Where there is vibration, solder makes the wire stiff, so it can break where the solder ends; crimped connections with strain relief are better there. Large power cables are joined with crimped lugs or connectors made for the size. In fire or high-heat areas, solder can melt. Where solder is used, the wire is first held mechanically, and the joint insulated with heat-shrink and supported.
markingPoints: Suitable for boards and small signal connections
Not in screw terminals (solder cold flow); use ferrules
Vibration: stiffening and breakage; crimps with strain relief
Large power cables use crimped lugs
Where used: mechanical hold, insulation and support

essays.stem: As team leader of a repair bench, explain the rules you would set for working with lead solder, flux fumes and hot irons, and how you would check that they are followed.
essays.modelAnswer: My rules would be: fume extraction switched on and placed near each joint; no eating, drinking or smoking at the bench and hands washed before breaks and at the end of the session, because of lead; safety glasses worn when soldering and cutting leads; irons always returned to their stands and never left on unattended; no flicking solder; boards isolated and capacitors discharged before work; and wrist straps tested before handling sensitive parts. Waste solder, dross and used braid go in a marked container. I would explain the reasons at a short briefing and post the rules at the bench. I would check by walking round during the session, looking at the strap test record and the extractor, and correcting anyone straight away. Repeated problems would be recorded and reported.
markingPoints: Fume extraction and lead hygiene rules
Eye protection, iron stands, no flicking solder
Isolation, capacitor discharge and ESD rules
Waste handling
Briefing, checks during work, correcting and recording

essays.stem: Explain how you would test a repaired control board before it goes back into service, from first checks to powered testing.
essays.modelAnswer: First I inspect the board visually under magnification for bridges, missed joints, wrong or reversed parts and flux left on. Then, with no power, I use a multimeter to check for short circuits across the supply rails and to check the resistance or continuity of the parts I changed. I then power the board from a current-limited bench supply set to its rated voltage, with a low current limit at first, and watch the current draw for signs of a short. If it is normal, I check the supply voltages on the board and the function of the repaired section, using the maker's test points or the service manual. Only when it passes do I refit it in the equipment, with the panel isolated, and do a final function test with the customer's system. I record the tests and results.
markingPoints: Visual inspection first
Unpowered meter checks for shorts and changed parts
Current-limited supply at rated voltage, watching the current
Checks voltages and function against the service information
Refits with the panel isolated, final test, records results

essays.stem: Describe how to look after soldering stations, tips and de-soldering tools, and explain how good care affects the quality of work.
essays.modelAnswer: I keep the tip clean on a damp sponge or brass wool and keep it tinned with a little solder, especially before putting the iron back in its stand. When the iron will not be used for a while, I turn it down or use its sleep mode. A tip that will not wet is cleaned with tip tinner, never filed or sanded, because that removes the plating. Worn or pitted tips are replaced. I check the real tip temperature with a tip thermometer at set times, and check the cable, stand and earth. De-soldering pumps are emptied and their seals cleaned, and vacuum desoldering tools have their filters and nozzles cleaned. Good care means heat flows quickly into the joint, so joints are made fast and wet properly, with less damage to boards and parts.
markingPoints: Clean and tin the tip; re-tin before parking
Sleep or turn down when idle
Never file plated tips; replace worn ones
Check temperature, cable and earth; maintain de-soldering tools
Explains the link between tool care and joint quality

practical1.title: Set up an ESD-safe bench and rework a circuit board
practical1.brief: As a group, set up an ESD-safe soldering bench (earthed mat, wrist straps tested and recorded, fume extraction, tip temperature checked). The assessor gives each pair a practice board with faults to rework: replace a multi-pin through-hole IC (or fit a socket), replace two through-hole parts the right way round, replace two two-ended surface-mount parts, clear planted solder bridges and repair one lifted track with a jumper wire. Each member does at least one through-hole and one surface-mount task while another member inspects their work. The group inspects every reworked joint under magnification against the assessor's written criteria, checks for shorts with a meter, and powers the board from a current-limited bench supply (12 V or less) only when the assessor agrees. Complete a rework record for each board. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Soldering stations with spare tips, tip thermometer
Desoldering pump, braid, flux pen and hot tweezers or hot-air tool
ESD mat, wrist straps and strap tester
Practice boards with planted faults and replacement parts
Magnifier or bench microscope, multimeter, current-limited bench supply
Rework record sheets and workmanship criteria
photos: The ESD bench set up, with the strap test record
The board before rework, showing the faults
The IC holes cleared before the new IC is fitted
The meter check for shorts and the powered test
checklist: Tested their wrist strap and used ESD controls throughout
Used the right tip, temperature and flux for each joint
Removed parts without lifting pads or damaging the board
Fitted parts the right way round with good joints on both sides
Fitted surface-mount parts and cleared bridges correctly
Inspected joints against the criteria and recorded results
Left the station tinned, off and in its stand, and the bench clean
safety: Use fume extraction; no eating or drinking at the bench; wash hands after
Wear safety glasses when soldering and cutting leads
Irons back in their stands at all times; never flick solder
Power boards only from a current-limited supply of 12 V or less, when the assessor agrees

practical2.title: Make, inspect and test a soldered wiring harness for a low-voltage control panel
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a drawing and wiring list for a small harness (for example a multi-pin connector to a terminal strip and a small control board, 12 V or 24 V). As a group, plan the work, then cut and strip the wires, solder them to the connector pins and terminal posts with the wire held mechanically first, fit heat-shrink sleeving and strain relief, and use crimped ferrules (not solder) where wires go into screw terminals. Each member makes at least four soldered connections and one crimped connection, and inspects another member's work. Test every wire for continuity and check for shorts between wires with a meter, then the assessor powers the finished assembly from a current-limited low-voltage supply for a function check. Complete a test sheet against the wiring list. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Harness drawing and wiring list from the assessor
Multi-core or single wires, multi-pin connector, terminal posts and terminal strip
Heat-shrink sleeving and a heat gun
Ferrules and ferrule crimper, cable ties
Multimeter, current-limited low-voltage supply, test sheet
photos: The plan and wiring list with roles
Wires held on terminal posts before soldering
Soldered connector pins before the sleeving goes on
Heat-shrink fitted and strain relief in place
Crimped ferrules in the screw terminals
checklist: Followed the wiring list and identified every wire
Held each wire mechanically before soldering
Made smooth, well-wetted joints without melted insulation
Fitted heat-shrink and strain relief correctly
Used crimped ferrules, not solder, in screw terminals
Tested continuity and shorts and recorded the results
Inspected another member's work and reported faults
safety: Use fume extraction and wash hands after soldering
Slide heat-shrink well away from the joint while soldering; keep the heat gun pointed away from people
Wear safety glasses when cutting and soldering
No mains supply on the harness; only the assessor applies the low-voltage test supply
